'''Robert Dirks''' (May 29, 1978 – February 3, 2015) was an American chemist known for his theoretical and experimental work in [[DNA nanotechnology]]. Born in [[Thailand]] to a [[Thai Chinese]] mother and American father, he moved to [[Spokane, Washington]] at a young age.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-02-05 |title=Robert Dirks, the LC grad who died in train crash, was a family man with 'unusual talent' |url=https://www.spokesman.com/stories/2015/feb/05/robert-dirks-lc-grad-who-died-train-crash-was-fami/ |access-date=2025-05-19 |website=Spokesman.com |language=en}}</ref> Dirks was the first graduate student in [[Niles Pierce]]'s research group at the [[California Institute of Technology]], where his [[dissertation]] work was on algorithms and computational tools to analyze [[nucleic acid thermodynamics]] and [[nucleic acid structure prediction|predict their structure]]. He also performed experimental work developing a biochemical [[Biochemical cascade|chain reaction]] to [[self-assembly|self-assemble]] nucleic acid devices.  Dirks later worked at [[D. E. Shaw Research]] on algorithms for [[protein folding]] that could be used to design new pharmaceuticals.

In February 2015, Dirks died in the [[Valhalla train crash]], the deadliest accident in the history of [[Metro-North Railroad]]. An award for early-career achievement in molecular programming research was established in his honor.

== Early life ==

Dirks was born in [[Bangkok, Thailand]], in 1978.<ref name="Bloomberg obit">{{cite news|last=Miller|first=Stephen|title=Robert Dirks, Scientist at D.E. Shaw Research, Dies at 36|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2015-02-05/robert-dirks-chemist-at-d-e-shaw-research-dies-at-36-in-crash|work=[[Bloomberg News]]|date=February 5, 2015|access-date=April 5, 2015}}</ref> His mother Suree, a [[Thai Chinese]] woman who worked in a bank at the time, his father, Michael Dirks, was a mathematics teacher at the [[International School Bangkok]] recruited from the United States.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.spokesman.com/stories/2008/nov/29/geithners-interest-in-math-started-as-teen/|title=Geithner's interest in math started as teen|last=Dirks|first=Mike|date=2008-11-29|website=The Spokesman-Review|access-date=2016-06-13}}</ref><ref name="Newsday obit">{{cite news|last=Armaghan|first=Sarah|title=Robert Michael Dirks, one of five passengers killed in Metro-North crash, was accomplished scientist and devoted father|url=http://www.newsday.com/news/new-york/robert-michael-dirks-one-of-five-passengers-killed-in-metro-north-crash-was-accomplished-scientist-and-devoted-father-1.9908678|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150206004808/http://www.newsday.com/news/new-york/robert-michael-dirks-one-of-five-passengers-killed-in-metro-north-crash-was-accomplished-scientist-and-devoted-father-1.9908678|url-status=dead|archive-date=February 6, 2015|newspaper=[[Newsday]]|date=February 5, 2015|access-date=April 6, 2015}}</ref> After about a year, the family, including older<ref name="Newsday obit" /> brother William, moved back to [[Vancouver]], British Columbia, Canada so that his father could pursue doctoral studies in mathematics education at the [[University of British Columbia]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/three-victims-of-metro-north-crash-all-men-each-bringing-his-best-1423189608|title=Three Victims of Metro-North Crash: All Men, Each Bringing His Best|last1=Janos|first1=Adam|date=2015-02-06|last2=Morris|first2=Keiko|newspaper=Wall Street Journal|issn=0099-9660|access-date=2016-06-13}}</ref><ref name="Bangkok Post story">{{cite news|title=A life begun in Bangkok ends in fiery New York train wreck|url=http://www.bangkokpost.com/news/world/468257/a-life-begun-in-bangkok-ends-in-fiery-new-york-train-wreck|work=[[Bangkok Post]]|date=February 6, 2015|access-date=April 5, 2015}}</ref> Four years later the family settled in Michael's hometown of [[Spokane, Washington]], where he took a job teaching math at [[North Central High School (Spokane, Washington)|North Central High School]] and [[Spokane Falls Community College]].<ref name="Bloomberg obit" /><ref name="Spokesman obit" />

Robert attended [[Lewis and Clark High School]], where he excelled academically, entering and winning many math competitions. He was selected to do cardiovascular research at the [[University of Washington]] over the summer before his senior year. During that year, he received the top score of 5 on every [[Advanced Placement]] exam he took, and was chosen as class [[valedictorian]] in 1996.<ref name="Spokesman obit">{{cite news|last=Culver|first=Nina|title=Robert Dirks, the LC grad who died in train crash, was a family man with 'unusual talent'|url=http://www.spokesman.com/stories/2015/feb/05/robert-dirks-lc-grad-who-died-train-crash-was-fami/|newspaper=[[The Spokesman-Review]]|location=[[Spokane, Washington|Spokane, WA]]|date=February 5, 2015|access-date=April 5, 2015}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |title=Robert Dirks, Scientist at D.E. Shaw Research, Dies at 36 |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2015-02-05/robert-dirks-chemist-at-d-e-shaw-research-dies-at-36-in-crash |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231121015410/https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2015-02-05/robert-dirks-chemist-at-d-e-shaw-research-dies-at-36-in-crash |archive-date=2023-11-21 |access-date=2025-05-19 |work=Bloomberg.com |language=en |url-status=live }}</ref> Shortly after graduation Robert and three of his classmates were one of three high school winners of the [[ExploraVision]] national scientific contest, earning them and their families a trip to Washington, D.C. The topic of their project was the future of nanotechnology.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://m.spokesman.com/stories/1996/jun/16/francoise-kuester-chosen-gus-teacher-of-the-year/|title=Francoise Kuester Chosen Gu's Teacher Of The Year|last=Fernandez|first=Maisy|date=1996-06-16|publisher=The Spokesman-Review|access-date=2015-07-13|archive-date=2015-07-13|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150713082355/http://m.spokesman.com/stories/1996/jun/16/francoise-kuester-chosen-gus-teacher-of-the-year/}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.spokesman.com/stories/1996/mar/23/teens-are-cranked-on-atomic-energy-lewis-and/|title=Teens Are Cranked On Atomic Energy Lewis And Clark Students Honored For Vision Of How Nanotechnology Can Shape Future|last=Johnson|first=Carla K.|date=1996-03-23|website=Spokesman.com|access-date=2016-06-13}}</ref>

Although he had been accepted to the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]], he chose instead to attend [[Wabash College]] in [[Crawfordsville, Indiana]].<ref name="Spokesman obit" />  He graduated ''[[summa cum laude]]'' and with [[Phi Beta Kappa]] honors,<ref name="Shaw research bio">{{cite web|url=http://www.deshawresearch.com/people_c-b_dirks.html|title=Robert Dirks|publisher=[[D. E. Shaw Research]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150630005743/http://www.deshawresearch.com/people_c-b_dirks.html|archive-date=2015-06-30|access-date=April 6, 2015}}</ref> from Wabash in 2000<ref name="Bloomberg obit" /> with a [[Double majors in the United States|double major]] in chemistry and math.<ref name="Spokesman obit" />  He also did a two [[minor (academic)|minors]] in biology and music, playing the [[bassoon]], [[clarinet]] and [[piano]].<ref name="Spokesman obit" />

He then began graduate studies in chemistry at the [[California Institute of Technology]] in [[Pasadena, California]]. He received his [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] in 2005 and remained at Caltech for a [[postdoctoral fellowship]]. During his years there he met Christine Ueda, another doctoral student who became his wife.<ref name="Bloomberg obit" />

== Research ==
{{Multiple image|image1 = Mao-4armjunction-schematic.png|image2 = Pseudoknot.svg|footer = Dirks developed algorithms and computational tools for [[Nucleic acid structure prediction|predicting the structure]] and [[Nucleic acid thermodynamics|thermodynamics]] of certain classes of nucleic acid structures: those containing multiple strands ''(top)'' and [[pseudoknot]]s ''(bottom)''.|direction = vertical}}Dirks was the first graduate student in the laboratory of [[Niles Pierce]] at Caltech.<ref name="Spokesman obit" />  His [[doctoral dissertation|dissertation]] was entitled "Analysis, design, and construction of nucleic acid devices".<ref>{{cite thesis|last1=Dirks|first1=Robert|title=Analysis, design, and construction of nucleic acid devices|url=https://thesis.library.caltech.edu/1998/|publisher=California Institute of Technology|access-date=27 February 2015|date=2005|doi=10.7907/VZ43-FM66|type=phd}}</ref>

Dirks' work in [[computational chemistry]] involved creating algorithms and computational tools for the analysis of [[nucleic acid thermodynamics]] and [[nucleic acid structure prediction]].<ref name="pierce1">{{cite web|title = The Pierce Lab|url = http://www.piercelab.caltech.edu/|publisher = California Institute of Technology|access-date = 26 February 2015|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20150211101231/http://www.piercelab.caltech.edu/|archive-date = 11 February 2015}}</ref> Dirks wrote the initial code for the [[NUPACK]] suite of [[nucleic acid design]] and analysis tools,<ref name="pierce2">{{cite web|title = NUPACK: Nucleic Acid Package|url = http://www.nupack.org/|publisher = California Institute of Technology|access-date = 26 February 2015|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20150223040305/http://www.nupack.org/|archive-date = 23 February 2015}}</ref> which generates [[base pairing]] probabilities through calculation of the statistical [[Partition function (statistical mechanics)|partition function]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|title = Prediction and design of DNA and RNA structures|last = Andersen|first = Ebbe Sloth|date = 2010|journal = New Biotechnology|doi = 10.1016/j.nbt.2010.02.012|pmid = 20193785|volume = 27|issue = 3|pages = 184&ndash;193}}</ref> Unlike other structure prediction tools, NUPACK is capable of handling an arbitrary number of interacting strands rather than being limited to one or two. Dirks also developed an algorithm capable of efficiently handling certain types of [[pseudoknot]]s, a class of structure that is more computationally intensive to analyze, although NUPACK only implements this ability for single RNA strands.<ref name=":0"/><ref>{{Cite journal|title = Multi-Strand RNA Secondary Structure Prediction and Nanostructure Design including Pseudoknots|last1 = Bindewald|first1 = Eckart|date = 2011|journal = ACS Nano|doi = 10.1021/nn202666w|pmid = 22067111|pmc = 3263976|last2 = Afonin|first2 = Kirill|last3 = Jaeger|first3 = Luc|last4 = Shapiro|first4 = Bruce A.|volume = 5|issue = 12|pages = 9542–9551}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|title = Advances in RNA Structure Prediction from Sequence: New Tools for Generating Hypotheses about Viral RNA Structure-Function Relationships|last = Schroeder|first = Susan J.|date = 2009|journal = Journal of Virology|doi = 10.1128/JVI.00251-09|pmid = 19369331|volume = 83|issue = 13|pages = 6326&ndash;6334|pmc=2698544}}</ref>

His experimental work pioneered the [[Nucleic acid hybridization|hybridization]] [[Biochemical cascade|chain reaction]] method, the first demonstration of the self-assembly of nucleic acid structures conditional on a molecular input.<ref name="pierce1" /> The method arose from attempts to use DNA [[Stem-loop|hairpins]] as "fuel" for [[DNA machine]]s, but Dirks and Pierce realized that they could instead be used for signal amplification, and when used in conjunction with an [[aptamer]], as a [[biosensor]].<ref>{{Cite journal|title = Hybridization chain reaction|last = Evenko|first = Daniel|date = 2004|journal = Nature Methods|doi = 10.1038/nmeth1204-186a|volume = 1|issue = 3|pages = 186&ndash;187|s2cid = 619697|doi-access = free}}</ref> As an enzyme-free, isothermal method, it later found application as the basis of an [[immunoassay]] method,<ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1039/C4AN00190G| pmid = 24828400| title = Hybridization chain reaction-based fluorescence immunoassay using DNA intercalating dye for signal readout| journal = The Analyst| volume = 139| issue = 13| pages = 3378–83| year = 2014| last1 = Deng | first1 = Y. | last2 = Nie | first2 = J. | last3 = Zhang | first3 = X. H. | last4 = Zhao | first4 = M. Z. | last5 = Zhou | first5 = Y. L. | last6 = Zhang | first6 = X. X. | bibcode = 2014Ana...139.3378D| s2cid = 26110015}}</ref> for [[in situ hybridization|''in situ'' hybridization]] imaging of [[gene expression]],<ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1021/nn405717p| pmid = 24712299| title = Next-Generation ''in Situ'' Hybridization Chain Reaction: Higher Gain, Lower Cost, Greater Durability| journal = ACS Nano| pages = 4284–4294| year = 2014| last1 = Choi | first1 = H. M. T. | last2 = Beck | first2 = V. A. | last3 = Pierce | first3 = N. A. | volume=8| issue = 5| pmc = 4046802}}</ref> and as the basis for catalytic, isothermal self-assembly of DNA nanostructures.<ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1038/nature06451| title = Programming biomolecular self-assembly pathways| journal = Nature| volume = 451| issue = 7176| pages = 318–322| year = 2008| last1 = Yin | first1 = P. | last2 = Choi | first2 = H. M. T. | last3 = Calvert | first3 = C. R. | last4 = Pierce | first4 = N. A. | pmid=18202654| bibcode = 2008Natur.451..318Y| s2cid = 4354536| url = https://authors.library.caltech.edu/74529/2/nature06451-s1.pdf}}</ref>

Dirks then worked at [[D. E. Shaw Research]] in [[Manhattan]] to develop methods for computational [[protein structure prediction]]<ref>{{cite news|last1=Yee|first1=Vivian|title=The Lives of 3 Crash Victims Who Shared a Metro-North Routine|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/02/06/nyregion/looking-at-lives-of-3-crash-victims-who-shared-train-routine.html|access-date=27 February 2015|date=5 February 2015|newspaper=The New York Times}}</ref> for the [[Drug design|design of new drugs]], beginning in 2006.<ref name="Bloomberg obit"/>

==Later life and death==

Dirks and Ueda married in 2007. She initially also worked at D. E. Shaw Research, but stopped in 2010 to raise the first of two children. The couple settled in the [[Westchester County, New York|Westchester County]] suburb of [[Chappaqua, New York]]. He rose early to commute to his job via [[Metro-North Railroad]]'s [[Harlem Line (Metro-North)|Harlem Line]], and returned late but devoted as much time as possible on evenings and weekends to his children.<ref name="Spokesman obit" />

On February 3, 2015, Dirks died in the [[Valhalla train crash]].  He was riding home in the front car of his train, which his brother says he likely did to take advantage of the quieter atmosphere,<ref name="Newsday obit" /> when it struck an SUV at a [[grade crossing]] north of [[Valhalla, New York|Valhalla]], {{convert|5|mi}} south of the [[Chappaqua (Metro-North station)|Chappaqua station]]. The train dragged the SUV while it came to a stop, loosening segments of the [[third rail]] that accumulated in the front car. Dirks, the SUV driver, and four other passengers were killed, making it the deadliest accident in Metro-North's history.<ref name="NYT train crash story">{{cite news|last1 = Santora|first1 = Marc|last2 = Flegenheimer|first2 = Matt|newspaper = New York Times|title = Investigation Underway in Metro-North Train Crash|url = https://www.nytimes.com/2015/02/05/nyregion/metro-north-train-crash.html|date = February 4, 2015|access-date = April 7, 2015}}</ref>

Reactions to his death came from many quarters, many paying tribute to his scientific prowess. His father recalled that "he always got everything the first time. He always excelled." Greg Sampson, Dirks' math teacher at Lewis and Clark, remembered when his student had finished an advanced class in [[trigonometry]] in just two weeks, something no other student of his has ever done, saying "he was just an amazing, amazing student." Niles Pierce recalled how Dirks was willing to take a chance on working with a younger professor. His former postdoc was, he said, "an unusual student, even for Caltech... He did remarkable things."<ref name="Spokesman obit" /> D. E. Shaw Research, his employer, called him "a brilliant scientist who made tremendous contributions to our own research, and to the broader scientific community."<ref name="Bloomberg obit" />

In April 2015, the [[International Society for Nanoscale Science, Computation, and Engineering]] (ISNCSE), the main [[scientific society]] for DNA nanotechnology and DNA computing, established the Robert Dirks Molecular Programming Prize to recognize early-career scientists for molecular programming research.<ref name="Award establishment">{{Cite web|url = http://blog.wabash.edu/alumninews/2015/05/01/robert-dirks-00-memorial-prize-announced/|title = Robert Dirks '00 memorial prize announced|date = 1 May 2015|access-date = 5 May 2015|publisher = Wabash College}}</ref>  The first prize was awarded in 2016.  As of June 2016, fundraising to establish a $100,000 [[Financial endowment|endowment]] was ongoing.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://dirksprize.caltech.edu/|title=The Dirks Prize Fund|publisher=California Institute of Technology|access-date=2016-06-13}}</ref>
